subject: Dedicated capacity pricing qualification
messages:

Subject: Post-call recap: Dedicated capacity pricing next steps

Thanks for your time today — quick recap and next steps from our discovery call: 

Key takeaways:
- Target workload: mixed chat + long-form generation for AI assistant and summarization pipelines.
- Estimated token volumes (per month): 150M prompt tokens + 450M generated tokens (600M total).
- Desired latency SLO: p95 < 300ms for interactive flows; background jobs can tolerate higher latency.
- Security: VPC peering + SOC 2 compliance required.

Open items we promised to follow up on:
1) Provide dedicated capacity pricing based on your target 600M tokens/mo and budget range.
2) Map those volumes to recommended GPU types, reserved capacity sizes, and throughput targets.
3) Share sample unit-economics (cost per 1M tokens) for the primary GPU options.

Next steps:
- I'll send a short pricing note and a couple of configuration options (GPU types and reserved sizes) — aim to get that over by EOD tomorrow.
- Please confirm whether the 600M tokens/mo is a firm forecast or a high-growth estimate (50%+ upside).

Attachments: placeholder pricing deck will follow in the next email.

Thanks,

Thanks Marissa — quick clarifications: 

- The 600M tokens is our current mid-point estimate for Q3 (we see a seasonal uptick). Planning range is 400M–900M tokens/mo depending on feature adoption.
- Budget: our procurement team is targeting an all-in committed spend in the $40k–$80k/mo range for dedicated capacity (including any reserved GPU costs + support).
- Target unit economics: we're looking for ballpark cost that gets us under $1,000 per 1M tokens ideally (we know this depends on model/perf).

Also: can you confirm whether reserved capacity billing is monthly and if burst capacity is included/charged separately? Procurement will need that for their internal comparison.

Appreciate the quick follow-up.

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Jenkins <alex.jenkins@acme.com>
Cc: SaaS Procurement <procurement@acme.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-04-29T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Dedicated capacity pricing next steps

Great — thanks for the ranges, Alex. Below is a concise pricing sketch and unit-economics for the two most common Dedicated configurations we recommend for workloads like yours. I attached a short PDF with the tables and assumptions.

Assumptions:
- Workload profile: 25% interactive (low-latency p95 targets), 75% batch/generation.
- Model baseline: 13B family (open checkpoint) for primary traffic; considerations for 33B in peak/offload scenarios.
- Measurement: tokens = prompt + generated.

Option A — Cost-optimized (A100 80GB-like equivalent):
- GPU: 4x A100-class instances reserved (private pool).
- Reserved capacity monthly list: $35k
- Throughput estimate: ~15–20M tokens/day (450–600M tokens/mo sustained) depending on batching.
- Unit cost: approximately $800–$950 per 1M tokens (depends on batching and cache hit rates).

Option B — Latency-optimized (H100 80GB-class equivalent):
- GPU: 4x H100-class instances reserved (higher perf for attention & kv-cache ops).
- Reserved capacity monthly list: $55k
- Throughput estimate: ~25–30M tokens/day (750–900M tokens/mo sustained).
- Unit cost: approximately $700–$850 per 1M tokens (better perf reduces tokens/sec cost at p95 targets).

Billing notes:
- Reserved capacity is billed monthly as a commitment. Burst/spot capacity for spikes is available but charged separately by the hour when used. We can include a 10% burst buffer in the contract to simplify procurement.

Example math (Option A):
- $35,000 / 600M tokens = $58.33 per 1M tokens base cost for capacity; additional per-request service and storage pushes all-in closer to the ranges above once you account for replication/ops. The quoted $800–$950/1M assumes production-grade redundancy + observability and realistic batching.

Action items for you so we can firm up the proposal:
1) Confirm whether the 400M–900M range above is acceptable (and whether a 10% burst buffer is acceptable).
2) Tell us if low-latency (p95 <300ms) is a hard requirement across all interactive flows or only critical subsets.
3) Let us know your preferred GPU class (A100-like vs H100-like) or if you want a mixed pool.

I’ve attached: Redwood_Dedicated_Pricing_1M_tokens.pdf — includes detailed tables and assumptions. I’ll loop Marcus for the technical sizing recs below.

Thanks,
Marissa
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
To: Alex Jenkins <alex.jenkins@acme.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Cc: SaaS Procurement <procurement@acme.com>
Date: 2027-04-29T11:35:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity pricing qualification — GPU & throughput recommendations

Hi Alex — Marcus from Infra sizing here. A few practical recommendations to translate Marissa’s options into an implementation-ready config: 

Recommendation summary:
- If you prioritize cost and your peak concurrency is moderate (<=150 concurrent interactive users), go with Option A (4x A100-class). Add a small standby H100 node for burst workloads if you expect occasional heavy attention workloads.
- If you need consistent sub-300ms p95 for high concurrency (200+ concurrent interactive users), pick Option B (4x H100-class) or increase to 6x H100-class to headroom for autoscaling.

Throughput/size guidance (expected sustained):
- 4x A100-class reserved: ~450–650M tokens/mo (good fit for your 400M–700M base range).
- 4x H100-class reserved: ~700–950M tokens/mo (good fit if you hit the upper end of 900M and want headroom).

SLA / Burst policy:
- We recommend a 10% reserved burst buffer included in the commitment for predictable billing (we can model this into the $/mo).

Next technical step:
- If you can confirm projected 90-day ramp (e.g., steady 600M or 400->900M ramp), I’ll produce a formal sizing diagram (CPU/node counts, network, KV cache policies, and expected p95 numbers) and a YAML config for Dedicated capacity that your infra team can review.

I can also join a quick 30-min technical call with your engineering lead next week if that helps accelerate procurement.

— Marcus
